# The Orionids and the God Who Sows

## Scripture

*"Those who sow with tears will reap with songs of joy. Those who go out weeping, carrying seed to sow, will return with songs of joy, carrying sheaves with them."* — Psalm 126:5–6 (NIV)

## Reflection

Each October, Earth drifts through the dusty trail of Halley's Comet, and the Orionid meteors streak across the autumn sky. Here is the wonder of it: those bright flashes are not the comet itself, long departed, but the debris it left behind—tiny grains that ignite into glory when they meet our atmosphere.

The psalmist knew something of this. He wrote of sowing in tears—of seasons when faithfulness feels like scattering seed into cold ground with no promise of harvest. Yet he insists that the weeping sower returns with sheaves, singing.

The Orionids remind us that God wastes nothing. The comet's passage seemed like a brief blaze and a departure, yet its trail still lights our skies centuries later. Likewise, the tears we sow in faithful obedience—the prayers whispered in hard seasons, the kindness offered when no one notices—these leave a trail of light we cannot yet see. God gathers what we scatter. He turns our weeping into harvest.

Autumn itself preaches this: leaves fall, fields empty, and everything seems to die. But the farmer knows the dying is the seed-bed of the reaping. So it is with faith. What feels like loss in October may be the very grain God is storing for joy.

Look up tonight. The meteors are proof: even dust, in God's hands, becomes light.

## Prayer

Lord of the harvest, when our sowing feels like weeping, remind us that You waste nothing. Turn our tears into seed and our waiting into sheaves, until we return with songs of joy. In Jesus' name, amen.
